rt.x: Section 2: The Kinematic Dyad: Speed and Velocity

With the foundational understanding of scalars and vectors established, it is now possible to apply this framework to the description of motion. The terms "speed" and "velocity," often used interchangeably in everyday conversation, hold distinct and precise meanings in physics.⁴ This distinction is not merely a matter of pedantry; it is fundamental to accurately describing and predicting the motion of objects. The greatest barrier to student understanding is often the need to unlearn the colloquial, imprecise use of these terms and adopt their rigorous scientific definitions.
2.1 Defining Speed: The Scalar Rate of Motion
Speed

is formally defined as a scalar quantity that describes the rate at which an object covers distance.³ In the context of the iGCSE syllabus, it is most simply defined as the distance travelled per unit of time.¹ Being a scalar, speed provides only a magnitude—it tells us "how fast" an object is moving but offers no information about its direction of travel.³

For example, if a car's speedometer reads 50 km/hr, this value represents the car's instantaneous speed. It is a complete description of the car's speed at that moment.¹¹ However, this information alone does not tell us whether the car is traveling north on a highway, turning a corner, or driving in reverse. It only quantifies the rate at which the car is covering its path.
2.2 The Foundational Prerequisite: Distance vs. Displacement
The fundamental reason for the difference between speed and velocity lies in the distinction between two other quantities:
distance
and
displacement
.¹⁰ Understanding this pair is a prerequisite for mastering the concepts of speed and velocity.
Distance (s)

is a scalar quantity that represents the total length of the path an object has travelled. It is the cumulative measure of "how much ground has been covered".¹⁰ If an object moves from point A to point B and then to point C, the total distance is the length of the path A to B plus the length of the path B to C. Distance can only be a positive value or zero.
Displacement (Δx or s)

is a vector quantity that represents the object's overall change in position. It is defined as the straight-line distance and direction from the object's initial position to its final position.³ Displacement is concerned only with the starting and ending points, not the path taken between them.
Consider a practical example: A person walks 4 meters East, then turns and walks 3 meters North.
The
distance
travelled is the sum of the path lengths:
The
displacement

. To be a complete vector, the direction must also be specified (e.g., 36.9 degrees North of East).

This example clearly shows that the magnitude of the displacement is not necessarily equal to the distance travelled. They are only equal if the object moves in a straight line without changing direction.
2.3 Defining Velocity: The Vector Rate of Motion
Building directly upon the concept of displacement,
velocity

is defined as the vector rate of motion. More precisely, it is the rate of change of an object's displacement.⁴ As a vector quantity, velocity must be described with both a magnitude and a direction.³ The magnitude of the velocity vector is, by definition, the object's instantaneous speed.
Therefore, the definition provided by the iGCSE syllabus—"speed in a given direction"—is a perfect and concise summary of the concept.¹
Let's revisit the earlier example of the car:
"The car is travelling at 50 km/hr" describes its
speed
"The car is travelling at 50 km/hr West" describes its
velocity
. This statement is more comprehensive as it tells us not only how fast the car is moving but also where it is going.⁴
The direction of the velocity vector is always the same as the direction of the object's motion at that instant.
Section 3: Mathematical Formulation and Calculation

The conceptual differences between speed and velocity are reflected directly in the formulas used to calculate them. Average speed is derived from the total distance travelled, a scalar, while average velocity is derived from the net displacement, a vector. This mathematical distinction provides a powerful tool for analyzing motion and resolving apparent paradoxes, such as how an object can move for a significant amount of time and have an average velocity of zero.
3.1 Calculating Average Speed

Average speed is a measure of the overall rate of motion for an entire journey, without regard to variations in speed or changes in direction along the way. It is calculated by dividing the total distance travelled by the total time taken for the journey.¹
The formula is:

3.2 Calculating Average Velocity
Average velocity describes the overall rate at which an object's position has changed over a time interval. It is calculated by dividing the total displacement by the total time taken.¹¹
The formula is:

Section 4: The Conceptual Crucible: Velocity in the Real World

Applying the definitions of speed and velocity to real-world scenarios is the ultimate test of comprehension. The motion of objects, from cars on a road to planets in orbit, can only be fully understood through the lens of vector analysis. This section explores velocity in both linear and circular motion, culminating in an analysis that reveals the profound link between velocity, acceleration, and force.
4.1 Linear Motion: Constant and Changing Velocity
Motion in a straight line provides the simplest context for understanding velocity.
Constant Velocity

: An object is said to have a constant velocity if, and only if, both its speed and its direction of motion remain constant.⁴ This means the object must travel in a straight line without speeding up or slowing down. For example, a train moving at a steady 90 km/hr due North on a straight track has a constant velocity.
Changing Velocity
: An object moving in a straight line can still experience a change in velocity if its speed changes.
Speeding Up
: If a car starts from rest and travels in a straight line, its speed increases. Since its speed (the magnitude of its velocity) is changing, its velocity is changing.
Slowing Down
: If a driver applies the brakes while traveling in a straight line, the car's speed decreases. This change in speed also constitutes a change in velocity.¹⁴

In these linear cases, the use of positive and negative signs is particularly effective. If motion to the right is defined as positive, a car moving to the right with increasing speed has a positive velocity that is becoming more positive. A car moving to the right but slowing down has a positive velocity that is becoming less positive (approaching zero).
4.2 The Definitive Test: Uniform Circular Motion
The most powerful illustration of the difference between speed and velocity is the case of
uniform circular motion
: the motion of an object in a circular path at a constant speed.²¹ This scenario is a conceptual crucible because it forces a confrontation with the vector nature of velocity.
Scenario
: Imagine a race car driving around a perfectly circular track at a constant speed of 150 km/hr.⁴
Analysis
Is the speed constant?
Yes. The car's speedometer, which measures instantaneous speed, remains fixed at 150 km/hr. The magnitude of its motion is unchanging.²¹
Is the velocity constant?
No. Velocity is a vector, defined by both magnitude and direction. While the magnitude (speed) is constant, the car's direction of motion is continuously changing as it navigates the curve.²²
At the northernmost point of the track, the car's velocity is 150 km/hr, East.
At the westernmost point, its velocity is 150 km/hr, South.
At the southernmost point, its velocity is 150 km/hr, West.
At the easternmost point, its velocity is 150 km/hr, North.

At every single point on the circle, the direction of the velocity vector is different from the point before it.²⁵ The direction of the instantaneous velocity vector at any point on the circle is always
tangential
to the circle at that point.²⁰ This means the velocity vector points along a straight line that just touches the circle at the object's location.
This analysis leads to a critical and unavoidable conclusion. Because the car's velocity is constantly changing (due to the changing direction), the car is undergoing
acceleration

, even though its speed is constant. This realization is a cornerstone of physics and demonstrates why the distinction between speed and velocity is not just semantic but essential for understanding the underlying causes of motion. This leads directly to a fundamental causal chain in mechanics: a change in direction necessitates a change in velocity; a change in velocity is, by definition, an acceleration; and according to Newton's Second Law (
F=ma

), an acceleration can only be produced by a net force.²² Therefore, any object moving in a circle must have a net force acting on it, directed towards the center of the circle (a centripetal force), to continuously change its velocity. A student who fails to grasp that velocity is changing in this scenario cannot possibly understand why a force is required to make an object turn.

Acceleration
is formally defined as the rate at which an object's
velocity changes
over time.¹⁴ It is a vector quantity, meaning it has both magnitude and direction. The direction of the acceleration vector is the same as the direction of the change in the velocity vector.

5.2 The Three Ways to Accelerate
Because acceleration is defined as any change in velocity, and velocity has both magnitude (speed) and direction, there are three distinct ways an object can accelerate ²⁰:
By changing speed

: This is the most intuitive form of acceleration. An object that is speeding up (e.g., a sprinter leaving the starting blocks) or slowing down (e.g., a car braking for a stop sign) is accelerating. The term for slowing down is
deceleration
By changing direction

: As established with the uniform circular motion example, an object moving at a constant speed but changing its direction is accelerating.⁴ The steering wheel of a car is, therefore, an accelerator just as much as the gas pedal and the brake pedal are.²⁶

This comprehensive definition dismantles the common misconception that an object moving very fast is necessarily accelerating. An airplane flying at a constant 900 km/hr in a perfectly straight line has a constant velocity and, therefore,

Conclusion: The Vectorial View of the Universe

The definition of velocity as "speed in a given direction" is far more than a simple vocabulary item; it is a gateway to a sophisticated and powerful method of describing the physical world. This report has systematically deconstructed this definition, demonstrating that the inclusion of direction transforms the simple scalar concept of speed into the robust vector quantity of velocity. This distinction is not arbitrary but is necessitated by the nature of motion itself.

The journey from understanding distance to displacement, and subsequently from speed to velocity, lays the essential groundwork for all of classical mechanics. It is the key to deciphering why an object moving in a circle at a constant speed is accelerating, and consequently, why a force is required to maintain that motion. It provides the logical foundation for defining acceleration as any change in velocity—be it in speed, direction, or both. By mastering the principles laid out in this report—the nature of scalars and vectors, the precise mathematical formulations, and the application to real-world scenarios—an iGCSE student moves beyond a one-dimensional, scalar description of motion. They begin to adopt a more complete, predictive, and powerful vectorial understanding of the universe, a crucial step in their journey as a student of physics.
Section 1: Introduction to Physical Quantities: The Fundamental Distinction
1.1 Defining the Landscape: Scalar and Vector Quantities
In the study of physics, every measurable property of the universe, from the mass of a subatomic particle to the velocity of a galaxy, is described using
physical quantities
. At the most fundamental level, these quantities are classified into two distinct categories:
scalars
and
vectors
. This distinction is not merely a matter of terminology; it dictates the mathematical rules that govern these quantities and, consequently, shapes our entire understanding of physical laws.
A
scalar quantity
is a physical quantity that is fully described by a
magnitude

—a numerical value or size—alone. Scalars answer the question "how much?". Examples are abundant in both science and daily life: the mass of an apple (e.g., 0.15 kg), the duration of a lesson (e.g., 3600 seconds), the energy in a battery (e.g., 5000 joules), or the temperature of a room (e.g., 20 degrees Celsius). The defining characteristic of scalars is that they have no associated direction. The mathematics of scalars is the familiar arithmetic we use every day; they can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided using standard algebraic rules. For instance, combining a 3 kg mass with a 2 kg mass results in a total mass of 5 kg.
In contrast, a
vector quantity
is a physical quantity that requires both a
magnitude
and a
direction

for its complete description. Vectors answer the questions "how much?" and "which way?". A description of a vector is incomplete and often meaningless without specifying its direction. Consider the act of pushing a box: stating you are applying a push of 50 newtons is insufficient. The outcome depends entirely on whether you are pushing it north, south, up, or down.
Force

, therefore, is a quintessential vector. The iGCSE syllabus specifically identifies several key vector quantities that are foundational to the study of motion: force, weight, velocity, acceleration, and gravitational field strength.

The distinction between these two types of quantities represents a fundamental shift in the mathematical modeling of physical reality. While scalars can be managed with one-dimensional arithmetic, vectors demand the tools of multi-dimensional geometry and trigonometry. This is because combining vectors involves considering their orientation in space. A failure to appreciate this shift is a primary source of error in physics. For example, two forces of 5 N each acting on an object do not necessarily produce a total force of 10 N; they only do so if they act in precisely the same direction. If they act at an angle to each other, their combined effect—the
resultant
—will be less than 10 N. Mastering the concept of vectors is therefore synonymous with mastering a new, more sophisticated way of thinking mathematically about the world.
1.2 Visualizing Vectors: The Power and Precision of Arrows
To manage the dual nature of vectors (magnitude and direction), physicists employ a simple yet powerful graphical representation: an
arrow
. This convention allows for a clear and intuitive visualization of vector quantities.
The
length
of the arrow is drawn proportionally to the
magnitude

of the vector quantity. This proportionality is critical for comparing different vectors. For example, if one is representing forces, an arrow for a force of 4 N must be drawn to be precisely twice as long as an arrow representing a force of 2 N. This visual scaling immediately conveys the relative strengths of the forces involved.
The
direction
in which the arrow points, indicated by the arrowhead, represents the
direction
of the vector quantity. This could be a cardinal direction (e.g., North, East), an angle relative to a reference axis (e.g., 30 degrees above the horizontal), or simply "upwards" or "downwards."
In written equations, to distinguish a vector from a scalar, a small arrow is often placed above the symbol for the quantity, such as writing
F⃗
for force or
v⃗
for velocity. This notation serves as a constant reminder that the quantity's directional properties must be considered in any mathematical operation.
1.3 The Mathematical Implications: Beyond Simple Arithmetic
The directional nature of vectors means they cannot be combined using the simple rules of scalar arithmetic. The process of finding the total effect of two or more vectors is called
vector addition

, and it is a geometric process. While the full treatment of vector mathematics extends beyond the iGCSE curriculum, the foundational principle is that the orientation of vectors must be accounted for.
For iGCSE Physics, this is most commonly encountered when finding the
resultant force

, which is the single force that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting on an object combined. When forces act along the same straight line, the process is straightforward: forces in the same direction are added, and forces in opposite directions are subtracted. However, when forces act at an angle to one another, graphical methods such as the
"Head-to-Tail" (or Triangle) Method
or the
Parallelogram Method
are required to determine the resultant. This geometric approach underscores the fundamental difference from scalar addition and is a key skill in analyzing the forces that govern motion.

Section 2: Force – The Vector of Interaction
2.1 Defining Force: A Directed Push or Pull
Force
is formally defined as a push or a pull that, when acting on an object, can cause a change in that object's state of motion. This "change in motion" is what physicists call
acceleration
. A force can cause a stationary object to start moving, a moving object to speed up, slow down, or change its direction of travel.
Crucially, force is a
vector quantity
. To fully describe a force, one must state both its
magnitude
(how strong the push or pull is) and the
direction

in which it acts. For example, kicking a football involves applying a force. The subsequent motion of the ball depends not only on how hard it was kicked (magnitude) but also on the direction of the kick. The standard international (SI) unit for the magnitude of a force is the
newton (N)
, named in honor of Sir Isaac Newton. One newton is defined as the force required to give a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one meter per second squared (
1 N = 1 kg⋅m/s²
2.2 Newton's Second Law (F=ma): The Causal Link Between Force and Acceleration
The relationship between force, mass, and acceleration is quantified by one of the most important laws in all of physics:
Newton's Second Law of Motion
. The law states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass. This is expressed by the iconic equation:
F = ma
Where:
F
is the
resultant force
acting on the object, measured in newtons (N).
m
is the
mass
of the object, a scalar quantity measured in kilograms (kg).
a
is the
acceleration
of the object, measured in meters per second squared (m/s²).
It is vital to recognize this as a
vector equation
. The arrows above force and acceleration (
F⃗
a⃗
) signify their vector nature. This equation is not merely a formula for calculation; it is a profound statement of causality in the physical world. The resultant force vector,
F⃗
, is the direct cause of the acceleration vector,
a⃗
. They are not just correlated; one physically generates the other.
Because mass,
m
, is a positive scalar quantity, it can only scale the magnitude of the acceleration vector; it cannot alter its direction. Consequently, the direction of the effect (acceleration) must be
identical

to the direction of the cause (the resultant force). If you push a trolley to the north, it will accelerate to the north. This causal link is predictive and powerful. By identifying all the forces acting on an object and determining their vector sum (the resultant force), we can predict the exact direction of its change in motion. This principle underpins everything from calculating the trajectory of a thrown ball to designing the flight path of a spacecraft.
2.3 Resultant Forces: The Importance of Vector Summation

In most real-world scenarios, an object is subjected to multiple forces simultaneously. For example, a moving car experiences a forward thrust from the engine, opposing forces of air resistance and friction, an upward support force from the road, and the downward pull of its weight. To apply Newton's Second Law, we must first find the
resultant force
(also known as the net force). The resultant force is the
vector sum
of all the individual forces acting on the object. It is the single force that would have the same effect on the object's motion as all the actual forces combined.

For forces acting along a single line, calculation is simple. For example, a firework at takeoff might experience an upward thrust of 2.0 N and a downward weight of 0.4 N. The resultant force would be
upwards.
When the resultant force on an object is
zero
, the forces are said to be
balanced
. In this state of
equilibrium
, the object's acceleration is zero. According to Newton's First Law of Motion, this means the object will either remain at rest or continue to move at a
constant velocity

(constant speed in a straight line). An object reaching terminal velocity is a prime example of equilibrium, where the downward force of weight is perfectly balanced by the upward force of air resistance, resulting in zero resultant force and thus zero acceleration.
Section 3: Weight – The Vector of Gravity
3.1 The Critical Distinction: Mass (Scalar) vs. Weight (Vector)
One of the most persistent and fundamental misconceptions in introductory physics is the confusion between
mass
and
weight

. In everyday language, the terms are often used interchangeably, but in physics, they represent distinct and different concepts. A clear understanding of this difference is essential and hinges on the distinction between scalars and vectors.
Mass (m)
is defined as the measure of the amount of matter within an object. It is a fundamental property of that object. Mass is a
scalar quantity
; it is fully described by its magnitude and has no direction. The SI unit for mass is the
kilogram (kg)
. An object's mass is
intrinsic
and
constant

, meaning it does not change regardless of the object's location in the universe. An astronaut with a mass of 70 kg on Earth will have the same 70 kg mass on the Moon, on Mars, or in the vacuum of deep space. Mass is also a measure of
inertia
—an object's resistance to changes in its state of motion.
Weight (W)
, in contrast, is defined as the
force of gravity
acting on an object's mass. Because it is a force, weight is a
vector quantity
. It possesses both magnitude and direction. The SI unit for weight is the
newton (N)

. The direction of the weight vector is always attractive, pointing towards the center of the celestial body creating the gravitational field (e.g., towards the center of the Earth). Unlike mass, an object's weight is
not constant
; it depends on the strength of the local gravitational field. The same 70 kg astronaut would weigh significantly less on the Moon than on Earth because the Moon's gravitational pull is weaker.
3.2 The Weight Equation (W=mg): Quantifying the Force of Gravity
The relationship between weight, mass, and the strength of the local gravitational field is described by a simple and powerful equation:
W = mg
Where:
W
is the
weight
, a vector force measured in newtons (N).
m
is the
mass
, a scalar quantity measured in kilograms (kg).
g
is the
gravitational field strength
, a vector quantity measured in newtons per kilogram (N/kg).
The gravitational field strength,
g
, is a measure of the gravitational force exerted per unit of mass at a specific location. On the surface of the Earth, its magnitude is approximately
9.8 N/kg
, often rounded to
10 N/kg
for iGCSE calculations. This means that for every kilogram of mass, the Earth exerts a gravitational force of about 10 newtons. The direction of the vector
g
is downwards, towards the Earth's center.
This equation reveals a deep consistency within physical laws. It is, in fact, a specific, localized application of the more fundamental law, Newton's Second Law (
F=ma

). When an object is in free fall, the only significant force acting on it is the force of gravity, which we call weight (W). The acceleration it experiences under this force is called the acceleration of free fall, which is given the symbol
g
. By substituting the specific force
W
for the general force
F
, and the specific acceleration
g
for the general acceleration
a
, the universal law
F=ma
transforms into the specific case
W=mg
. This demonstrates that the physics governing a falling apple (
W=mg
) is identical to the principle governing a pushed trolley (
F=ma
). It is not a separate rule to be memorized but a logical consequence of a universal law.
Section 4: Velocity – The Vector of Motion
4.1 The Critical Distinction: Speed (Scalar) vs. Velocity (Vector)

In everyday conversation, "speed" and "velocity" are used as synonyms. In physics, however, they have precise and distinct meanings that are crucial for accurately describing motion. The difference lies entirely in the concept of direction, making one a scalar and the other a vector.
Speed
is a
scalar quantity

that describes the rate at which an object covers distance, or more simply, "how fast an object is moving". It is defined only by its magnitude, for example, 30 m/s or 100 km/h. Because it is a scalar, speed provides no information about the direction of motion.
Velocity
is a
vector quantity

that describes the rate at which an object's position changes. It is defined as "speed in a given direction". To specify an object's velocity, both its magnitude (the speed) and its direction of motion must be stated. For example, a complete description of velocity would be "30 m/s East" or "-20 m/s" (where the negative sign indicates motion in the opposite direction to a predefined positive direction). Two cars travelling on a motorway at the same speed of 100 km/h, but one travelling north and the other south, have the same speed but different velocities.
4.2 Displacement: The Vector Counterpart to Distance
To fully grasp the difference between speed and velocity, one must first understand the difference between their foundational quantities:
distance
and
displacement
Distance
is a
scalar quantity

representing the total path length an object has traveled between two points. It is the measure of "how much ground has been covered." For example, if a person walks 3 km north and then turns around and walks 4 km south, the total distance they have traveled is
3 km + 4 km = 7 km
Displacement
, on the other hand, is a
vector quantity

that represents the object's overall change in position. It is the straight-line separation from the starting point to the finishing point, and it includes the direction of that straight line. In the previous example, the person starts, goes 3 km north, and then 4 km south. Their final position is 1 km south of their starting point. Therefore, their displacement is
1 km South
. The actual path taken is irrelevant to the final displacement.
4.3 The Velocity Equation (v=s/t): Calculating with Direction
The definitions of speed and velocity lead to their respective formulas for calculating average values over a period of time.
The formula for average speed uses the scalar quantity,
distance
Average speed = Total distance / Time taken
The formula for average velocity uses the vector quantity,
displacement
Average velocity (v) = Displacement (s) / Time taken (t)
The use of displacement (
s
) instead of distance is the key mathematical difference and ensures that velocity correctly accounts for the direction of motion.
4.4 Case Study: Motion in a Circle – Constant Speed, Changing Velocity

The distinction between speed and velocity is most powerfully illustrated by considering an object moving in a circle at a constant speed, such as a satellite in orbit or a car navigating a roundabout.
An observer looking at the car's speedometer would see a constant reading, for example, 30 km/h. This means its
speed
(the magnitude of its motion) is
constant
However, the car's
direction
is
continuously changing
as it moves around the curve. At one moment it might be heading north, a moment later north-west, then west, and so on.
Because velocity is a vector composed of both magnitude (speed) and direction, and the direction is changing, the car's
velocity is also continuously changing

, even though its speed is constant. This seemingly subtle point is, in fact, a critical conceptual gateway. It leads directly to the understanding of acceleration in non-linear motion. Since acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity, it follows logically that any object moving in a circular path
must be accelerating
. This non-intuitive but necessary conclusion is fundamental to understanding the forces required to maintain curved motion, from planetary orbits to the engineering of banked railway tracks.
Section 5: Acceleration – The Vector of Change
5.1 Defining Acceleration: The Rate of Change of Velocity
In physics,
acceleration
is rigorously defined as the rate at which an object's
velocity changes
over time. This definition is precise and powerful. Because velocity is a vector,
any change in velocity
—whether in its magnitude (speed), its direction, or both—constitutes an acceleration. Consequently, acceleration itself must be a
vector quantity
This definition expands the everyday meaning of "acceleration" from simply "speeding up" to encompass three distinct scenarios:
Speeding up
: If an object's speed increases, its velocity is changing, and it is accelerating. This is often called positive acceleration.
Slowing down
: If an object's speed decreases, its velocity is also changing. This is a form of acceleration, although it is commonly referred to as
deceleration
or negative acceleration.
Changing direction
: As established in the case of circular motion, if an object maintains a constant speed but changes its direction of travel, its velocity is changing, and therefore it is accelerating.

The vector nature of acceleration is what resolves the apparent paradox of how an object can be accelerating while its speed remains constant. It decouples the common-language concept of "speeding up" from the precise physical definition of "accelerating." A force is required not only to start, stop, or change the speed of an object but also simply to make it turn a corner. This is a direct consequence of Newton's Second Law: a resultant force is required to cause an acceleration, and an object turning a corner is, by definition, accelerating.
5.2 The Acceleration Equation (a = Δv/t): Analyzing Changes in Motion
The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using the following formula, which directly reflects its definition:
a = Δv / t = (v - u) / t
Where:
a
is the average
acceleration
, a vector measured in meters per second squared (m/s²).
Δv
is the
change in velocity
, a vector measured in meters per second (m/s).
v
is the
final velocity
u
is the
initial velocity
t
is the
time interval
over which the change occurs, a scalar measured in seconds (s).
The SI unit for acceleration,
m/s²
, can be read as "meters per second, per second." This reinforces the concept that acceleration measures how much the velocity (in m/s) changes every second.
5.3 The Direction of the Acceleration Vector

A common point of confusion is the direction of the acceleration vector. The acceleration vector does not necessarily point in the same direction as the object's motion (i.e., the direction of the velocity vector). Instead, the acceleration vector points in the direction of the
change in velocity (Δv)
This leads to several key outcomes:
Speeding up

: When an object is speeding up in a straight line, its final velocity vector is longer than its initial velocity vector, but in the same direction. The change in velocity, Δv, is also in that same direction. Thus, for an object speeding up, the acceleration vector is in the
same direction
as the velocity vector.
Slowing down

: When an object is slowing down in a straight line, its final velocity vector is shorter than its initial one. The change in velocity, Δv, points in the opposite direction to the motion. Therefore, for an object decelerating, the acceleration vector is in the
opposite direction
to the velocity vector.
Uniform Circular Motion

: For an object moving in a circle at a constant speed, the velocity vector is always tangent to the circle. However, to make the object turn, the change in velocity is always directed towards the center of the circle. Therefore, the acceleration vector (known as
centripetal acceleration
) is always directed
towards the center of the circle
, perpendicular to the velocity vector at any given instant. This acceleration is caused by a resultant force, also directed towards the center, known as the
centripetal force
Section 6: Gravitational Field Strength – The Vector Field
6.1 Defining 'g' as a Vector Quantity: Force per Unit Mass
The concept of a
field
is one of the most powerful ideas in physics. A field describes a property of space itself, where a particular type of object will experience a force. A
gravitational field
is a region of space where an object with mass experiences a force of gravity.
Gravitational field strength (g)
is a
vector quantity
that quantifies this field. It is defined as the gravitational force exerted per unit mass at a specific point in the field. As a vector, it has both magnitude and direction.
Magnitude
: The magnitude of
g
tells us the strength of the force on each kilogram of mass placed at that point. On Earth's surface, this is approximately
9.8 N/kg
Direction
: The direction of
g
is the direction of the gravitational force that a mass would experience, which is always
towards the center
of the larger mass creating the field.

The units of gravitational field strength, newtons per kilogram (N/kg), can be shown to be dimensionally equivalent to the units of acceleration, meters per second squared (m/s²). This is no coincidence; the gravitational field strength at a location is numerically equal to the acceleration of free fall at that location.
6.2 Visualizing the Field: Lines of Force
Gravitational fields are visualized using
gravitational field lines
. These are imaginary lines that map the field's properties:
The
direction
of the arrow on a field line indicates the direction of the gravitational force on a mass placed at that point. For a spherical body like a planet, these lines point radially inwards.
The
spacing

of the field lines represents the field's strength. Where the lines are closer together, the field is stronger; where they are further apart, the field is weaker. For a planet, the field is strongest near the surface and weakens with increasing distance.

The concept of a vector field is more fundamental than the older idea of "action at a distance." It proposes that a massive object, like the Earth, modifies the properties of the space around it, creating a gravitational field. This field then exists at every point in space, regardless of whether another mass is present. When a second object (like an apple) is placed in this field, it is the field at the apple's location that exerts the force on it. This "field-mediated" interaction is a cornerstone of modern physics, extending to the description of electric and magnetic forces as well.
6.3 How 'g' Dictates the Magnitude and Direction of Weight
The relationship between weight and the gravitational field is encapsulated in the equation
W = mg
. This can now be understood more deeply as a vector equation where the properties of the weight vector are determined entirely by the field.
The scalar mass,
m
, of an object is multiplied by the gravitational field vector,
g
, at its location. This product yields the weight vector,
W
. This means the gravitational field is the direct cause of the weight force. The field's magnitude (
g
) determines the weight's magnitude (
W
), and the field's direction determines the weight's direction. An object has weight because it is situated within a gravitational field.

velocity (v)

Conceptual Foundations of Acceleration
Beyond 'Speeding Up': Defining Acceleration in Physics

In the study of motion, or kinematics, precision in language is paramount. While in everyday conversation, "acceleration" is often used synonymously with "speeding up," its definition in physics is far more rigorous and encompassing. Formally,
acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity
.¹ This means that acceleration quantifies how much an object's velocity changes during each unit of time, typically every second.¹

The distinction between the colloquial and scientific definitions is a foundational concept. A performance car that goes from a standstill to 60 miles per hour is clearly accelerating. However, a car that applies its brakes to slow down is also accelerating. Furthermore, a race car maintaining a constant speed around a curved track is also undergoing acceleration. This is because the core of the definition rests on the term
velocity

, not speed. Understanding this distinction is the first step toward mastering the physics of motion. The central definition, which aligns with the iGCSE syllabus, is that acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time.³
The Vector Nature of Acceleration: Why Direction Matters
To fully grasp the concept of acceleration, one must first appreciate the nature of velocity. Velocity is a
vector quantity
, meaning it possesses both
magnitude
(how fast an object is moving, i.e., its speed) and
direction
.⁴ Since acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity, it logically follows that
acceleration must also be a vector quantity
, possessing its own magnitude and direction.⁶
This vector nature implies that an object undergoes acceleration if its velocity changes in any way. There are three distinct ways this can happen:
A change in speed (speeding up)
: The magnitude of the velocity vector increases.³
A change in speed (slowing down)
: The magnitude of the velocity vector decreases.³
A change in direction
: The direction of the velocity vector changes, even if its magnitude (speed) remains constant.³

A powerful illustration of the third case is an object in uniform circular motion, such as a satellite orbiting the Earth at a constant speed.⁶ Although its speed never changes, its direction of motion is continuously changing as it follows a curved path. Because its velocity vector is constantly changing direction, the satellite is in a perpetual state of acceleration, known as
centripetal acceleration
, which is directed towards the center of the circle.⁶ This example decisively refutes the common misconception that acceleration only involves a change in speed.

The direction of an object's acceleration is determined by the direction of the net force acting upon it, a principle formalized in Newton's Second Law of Motion.⁶ The acceleration vector points in the same direction as the vector representing the change in velocity (Δv).
Distinguishing Between Average and Instantaneous Acceleration
The iGCSE Physics syllabus primarily concerns itself with calculations of
average acceleration

. This is the total change in velocity divided by the total time interval over which that change occurs.³ The standard formula used at this level calculates this average value. This is particularly applicable in situations where acceleration is
uniform

, or constant, meaning the velocity changes by an equal amount in every equal time period.⁶ An object in freefall near the Earth's surface (neglecting air resistance) is a classic example of uniform acceleration.⁶
For a more complete understanding, it is useful to be aware of the concept of
instantaneous acceleration

. This is the acceleration of an object at a single, specific moment in time.⁶ In calculus, this is found by taking the derivative of the velocity function with respect to time, which is equivalent to finding the limit of the average acceleration as the time interval (Δt) approaches zero.⁶ While the mathematical tools for instantaneous acceleration are beyond the scope of the iGCSE curriculum, the concept helps clarify that the formula
a = Δv / t
provides an average value over a duration, which is identical to the instantaneous value at all times if the acceleration is uniform.
Deconstructing the Equation of Motion: a = Δv / t
The Core Formula and its Components

The mathematical relationship that defines acceleration is expressed in a concise and powerful equation. This formula is a cornerstone of kinematics and is essential for solving problems related to motion. The equation is:
Each component of this equation has a precise physical meaning ²:
a
represents
acceleration
. It is the quantity we are defining—the rate at which velocity changes.
Δv
represents the
change in velocity

. The Greek letter Delta (Δ) is a standard scientific symbol used to denote "change in" a particular quantity. Therefore, Δv is not a value in itself but represents the difference between two velocity states.
t
represents the
time taken
for the change in velocity to occur. In some contexts, this may be written as Δt to emphasize it is a time interval, but for iGCSE purposes,
t
is commonly used to represent this duration.²
Unpacking Δv: The Critical Role of Initial and Final Velocity (v and u)
The term
Δv

is the conceptual heart of the acceleration equation. It represents the transition of an object from an initial state of motion to a final state. To calculate this change, we must subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity.² The standard symbols used in iGCSE Physics for these velocities are:
u
for
initial velocity
(the velocity at the beginning of the time interval, t=0).
v
for
final velocity
(the velocity at the end of the time interval).

), takes a specific amount of time (

) to transition, and the agent of that change is the acceleration (
a
). Because velocity is a vector, the signs of

and

are critical. If an object reverses its direction, its initial and final velocities will have opposite signs. For example, a ball hitting a wall at +15 m/s and rebounding at −15 m/s has undergone a substantial change in velocity of

Algebraic Manipulation: Rearranging the Formula

A key skill in physics is the ability to manipulate equations to solve for any unknown variable. The acceleration formula can be rearranged to find the final velocity, initial velocity, or time, given the other quantities.¹⁸ A formula triangle can serve as a helpful visual aid for this process.²

The Language of Motion: Units and Dimensions
The SI Unit for Acceleration: Understanding Metres Per Second Squared (m/s²)
In the International System of Units (SI), which is the standard for all scientific work, every physical quantity has a specific base or derived unit. The SI unit for acceleration is
metres per second squared
, which is written as
m/s²
or, using negative index notation,
m·s⁻²
.²⁰

This unit has a direct physical interpretation that reinforces the definition of acceleration. It means "metres per second, per second".² An acceleration of, for example, 5 m/s² signifies that for every one second that passes, the object's velocity increases by 5 metres per second.²² If it starts from rest, after 1 second its velocity will be 5 m/s, after 2 seconds it will be 10 m/s, after 3 seconds it will be 15 m/s, and so on.
Deriving the Unit: A Dimensional Analysis
The unit for acceleration is not arbitrary; it is derived directly from its defining equation. This process, known as dimensional analysis, confirms the consistency of the physics.
The formula is:
Acceleration = Change in Velocity / Time
The SI unit for velocity is metres per second (m/s).²⁵
The SI unit for time is the second (s).²⁵
Substituting the units into the formula gives:
Unit of Acceleration = (m/s) / s
Mathematically, dividing by
s
is the same as multiplying by

This simple derivation shows how the unit m/s² logically emerges from the definition of acceleration.²¹

While m/s² is the required SI unit for calculations in iGCSE Physics, it is important to be aware that other units for acceleration exist and may be encountered in different contexts. Failure to do so will lead to an incorrect answer.²³
Direction and Sign: Mastering Positive and Negative Acceleration
Establishing a Frame of Reference: The Importance of a Coordinate System

Because acceleration is a vector, its direction is as important as its magnitude. To describe this direction mathematically, we use positive and negative signs. However, these signs are not absolute; their meaning is entirely dependent on the
coordinate system
or frame of reference that is chosen for a given problem.⁹
Before solving any problem involving vectors, one must first define which direction is
positive
. The standard convention, which will be used in all subsequent examples unless specified otherwise, is:
For horizontal motion
: Motion to the
right
is positive, and motion to the
left
is negative.
For vertical motion
: Motion
upwards
is positive, and motion
downwards
is negative.
Once this convention is established, the signs of velocity, displacement, and acceleration can be assigned consistently.²⁸
Positive Acceleration: Scenarios and Interpretations
Positive acceleration

simply means that the acceleration vector is pointing in the direction defined as positive in the coordinate system.¹¹ For example, if a car starts from rest and moves to the right (the positive direction), its velocity is positive and increasing. Since the change in velocity is positive, its acceleration is also positive.²⁸ Similarly, if an object is falling and the downward direction has been defined as positive, its acceleration due to gravity is considered positive.²⁹
Negative Acceleration and Deceleration: Addressing Common Misconceptions
The concept of
negative acceleration

is a frequent source of confusion. The most common error is to assume that negative acceleration always means an object is slowing down.⁹ This is incorrect. Negative acceleration simply means that the acceleration vector points in the direction defined as
negative
The term
deceleration
has a more specific meaning: it refers to an acceleration that is directed
opposite to the direction of the object's velocity

, causing its speed to decrease.² While deceleration often corresponds to a negative acceleration (e.g., a car moving to the right with positive velocity, braking with a leftward, negative acceleration), this is not always the case.
Consider an object that is already moving in the negative direction (to the left), so it has a negative velocity (e.g.,
u = −5 m/s
). If it experiences a negative acceleration (e.g.,
a = −2 m/s²
), this acceleration is in the
same direction
as its velocity. As a result, the object will
speed up
in the negative direction. After one second, its new velocity will be

. The velocity has become more negative, but its speed (the magnitude of velocity) has increased from 5 m/s to 7 m/s.⁹ This example clearly demonstrates that negative acceleration does not always cause slowing down.
The Interaction of Velocity and Acceleration Signs

The confusion surrounding signs can be entirely eliminated by understanding a single, definitive rule that governs the relationship between the signs of velocity and acceleration and the resulting change in an object's speed. The rule is based on whether the acceleration and velocity vectors point in the same or opposite directions.⁹
If acceleration and velocity have the
same sign
(both positive or both negative), the acceleration is acting in the same direction as the motion. The object will
speed up
If acceleration and velocity have
opposite signs
(one positive and one negative), the acceleration is acting in the opposite direction to the motion. The object will
slow down

Visualising Motion: Acceleration on Velocity-Time Graphs
The Gradient as Acceleration: A Graphical Definition

Velocity-time graphs are powerful tools in kinematics because they provide a complete visual narrative of an object's motion. On such a graph, time is plotted on the horizontal axis (x-axis) and velocity is plotted on the vertical axis (y-axis).³¹ The most important feature of this type of graph for the study of acceleration is its
gradient
, or slope.
The fundamental principle is:
The gradient of a velocity-time graph represents acceleration

.²⁶ This is not a coincidence but a direct graphical representation of the definition of acceleration. The gradient is calculated as the change in the y-axis ("rise") divided by the change in the x-axis ("run"). On a velocity-time graph, this corresponds to
rise = Δv
and
run = Δt
. Therefore,
gradient = Δv / Δt
, which is the definition of acceleration.³³
Interpreting the Slope
By inspecting the line on a velocity-time graph, one can deduce the nature of the object's acceleration without any calculation:
Positive, constant gradient
(a straight line sloping upwards): This indicates constant positive acceleration. The object is speeding up in the positive direction or slowing down in the negative direction.³¹
Negative, constant gradient
(a straight line sloping downwards): This indicates constant negative acceleration. The object is slowing down in the positive direction or speeding up in the negative direction.³¹
Zero gradient
(a horizontal line): This indicates zero acceleration. The object is moving at a constant velocity. If the horizontal line is on the time axis (v=0), the object is stationary.³¹
Steep gradient
: A steeper slope (either positive or negative) signifies a larger magnitude of acceleration; the velocity is changing rapidly.³¹
Gentle gradient
: A shallower slope signifies a smaller magnitude of acceleration; the velocity is changing more gradually.³¹
Curved line
: A curved line indicates that the acceleration is not uniform; it is changing over time. This is a topic typically explored beyond the iGCSE level.
Calculating Acceleration from a Velocity-Time Graph
To find a numerical value for acceleration from a velocity-time graph, one must calculate the gradient of the relevant section of the line.
Method
Choose two points on the straight-line segment of the graph. To improve accuracy, these points should be as far apart as possible.³¹
Draw a large "gradient triangle" connecting these two points, showing the "rise" (Δv) and the "run" (Δt).³¹
Read the values for the change in velocity (from the y-axis) and the change in time (from the x-axis).
Calculate the acceleration using the formula:
a = gradient = rise / run = Δv / Δt
For example, if a cyclist's velocity changes from 5 m/s to 15 m/s between the time markers of t=10 s and t=20 s, the acceleration would be:
a = 10 m/s / 10 s = 1 m/s²
Distinguishing Acceleration from Distance Travelled
It is crucial to remember that a velocity-time graph contains more information than just acceleration. While the gradient represents acceleration, the
area under the graph represents the distance travelled

(or displacement).²⁶ For a section of constant velocity, this area is a rectangle. For a section of constant acceleration, the area is a triangle or a trapezium. This dual nature makes velocity-time graphs an exceptionally information-rich tool for analyzing motion.
Synthesis and Advanced Perspectives
The Link to Forces: A Primer on Newton's Second Law
Thus far, this guide has focused on kinematics—the description of motion without considering its causes. However, it is important to understand that acceleration does not occur spontaneously.
Acceleration is caused by a net or resultant force
acting on an object.
This fundamental relationship is described by
Newton's Second Law of Motion
, which states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass. This is famously expressed by the equation
F = ma
, where
F
is the net force,
m
is the mass, and
a
is the acceleration.⁶ This principle bridges the gap from kinematics to dynamics (the study of the causes of motion) and explains that to change an object's velocity, a force is required.
Uniform Acceleration and the 'suvat' Equations
The problems and examples discussed have largely assumed uniform (constant) acceleration. This is a special but very common case in introductory physics. The equation
v = u + at
is the first of a set of five powerful equations, often called the
'suvat' equations
, that are used to solve any problem involving motion with constant acceleration.¹⁸ These equations relate the five key kinematic variables: displacement (
s
), initial velocity (
u
), final velocity (
v
), acceleration (
a
), and time (
t
). Mastering the concept of acceleration is the gateway to using this full suite of tools to analyze motion.
Summary of Key Concepts and Formulae
For effective revision, the core concepts of acceleration can be condensed into the following key points:
Definition
: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
Vector Nature
: Acceleration has both magnitude and direction. An object accelerates if its speed changes, its direction changes, or both.
Core Formula
: The average acceleration is calculated using
a = Δv / t
, which is practically applied as
a = (v - u) / t
SI Unit
: The standard unit for acceleration is metres per second squared (m/s²).
Sign Convention
: The key rule is: if velocity and acceleration have the same sign, the object speeds up; if they have opposite signs, the object slows down.
Velocity-Time Graphs
: On a velocity-time graph, the gradient of the line represents acceleration, and the area under the line represents the distance travelled.
Section 1: Foundational Principles of Acceleration

This section establishes the core concepts necessary for a nuanced understanding of acceleration. By moving beyond rote memorization of formulas, a robust conceptual framework is built, addressing the vector nature of motion and the often-misunderstood sign conventions that are critical for accurate analysis.
1.1 Defining Acceleration: The Rate of Change of Velocity
In physics, acceleration is formally defined as the
rate of change of velocity

.¹ This definition is crucial; it specifies that acceleration describes how much an object's velocity changes every second.² An object accelerates when its velocity changes, whether that change involves speeding up, slowing down, or altering its direction of motion.⁵
The fundamental formula used to calculate the average acceleration of an object is:
a = Δv / Δt
Where:
a
represents acceleration.
Δv
represents the change in velocity.
Δt
represents the time taken for this change to occur.⁷
The standard SI unit for acceleration is
metres per second squared
, written as
m/s²
or
m·s⁻²
.⁸ This unit can be conceptually understood as "metres per second, per second" (
m/s/s
), which clearly illustrates that acceleration is a measure of how the velocity (measured in m/s) is changing with each passing second.²
1.2 The Vector Nature of Motion: Why Velocity Matters More Than Speed
To fully grasp acceleration, it is essential to distinguish between scalar and vector quantities. A
scalar
quantity possesses only magnitude (a numerical value), such as distance or speed. A
vector
quantity, however, has both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, and acceleration.¹⁰
Acceleration is fundamentally defined by the change in
velocity
, not just speed.¹² This means an object can accelerate in three distinct ways:
By
speeding up
(changing the magnitude of its velocity).
By
slowing down
(changing the magnitude of its velocity).
By
changing its direction
of motion (even if its speed remains constant).¹³

A car travelling at a constant 50 km/h around a circular track has a constant speed, but because its direction is continuously changing, its velocity is also continuously changing. Therefore, it is accelerating.¹²

Within the iGCSE Co-ordinated Science syllabus, the term "speed-time graph" is commonly used. This is a simplification that is valid for the typical problems presented, which almost exclusively involve motion in a straight line without a change in direction. In this specific context, the magnitude of the velocity (speed) is the only component that changes, so the terms can be used interchangeably. However, it is more physically accurate to consider these as
velocity-time graphs

where the y-axis represents velocity in a single dimension. Understanding this distinction is vital for students who may progress to higher levels of physics, as it prevents the misconception that acceleration is only concerned with changes in speed.
1.3 The Sign Convention of Acceleration: Beyond "Speeding Up" and "Slowing Down"

A common oversimplification is that positive acceleration always means speeding up, and negative acceleration (often called deceleration or retardation) always means slowing down.² While this is frequently the case, it is not universally correct and can lead to significant errors in analysis. The effect of acceleration depends entirely on its direction relative to the object's velocity.
To analyze motion correctly, a
sign convention
must be established. Typically, motion to the
right
or
upwards
is considered
positive
, while motion to the
left
or
downwards
is considered
negative
.¹³ Acceleration is positive if it acts in the designated positive direction and negative if it acts in the negative direction.
The true relationship that determines whether an object speeds up or slows down is the interaction between the signs of velocity and acceleration:
If velocity and acceleration have the
same sign
(both positive or both negative), the object will
speed up
Example
: A car moving to the left (negative velocity) that is pushed further to the left (negative acceleration) will increase its speed in the negative direction. Its velocity becomes
more negative
(e.g., from −10 m/s to −15 m/s), but its speed (the magnitude) increases.¹³
If velocity and acceleration have
opposite signs
(one positive and one negative), the object will
slow down
Example

: A ball thrown upwards (positive velocity) is acted upon by gravity, which causes a downward acceleration (negative acceleration). The ball slows down as it rises.¹³ Similarly, a car moving to the right (positive velocity) that applies its brakes experiences a leftward acceleration (negative acceleration) and slows down.¹⁴
This nuanced understanding is crucial for correctly interpreting physical scenarios and graphical representations of motion.
1.4 Determining Acceleration from Given Data (Tables)

When motion data is presented in a table of speed (or velocity) and time values, the average acceleration over a specific interval can be calculated systematically. This process directly applies the definition of acceleration.
The procedure is as follows:
Step 1: Identify the Interval
. The problem will specify the time interval for which the acceleration is to be calculated (e.g., between
t=2 s
and
t=5 s
).¹⁶
Step 2: Find the Change in Velocity (Δv)
. This is calculated by subtracting the initial velocity (
u
) from the final velocity (
v
). The initial velocity is the value at the start of the interval, and the final velocity is the value at the end.¹⁶ The formula is
Δv = v − u
Step 3: Find the Time Taken (Δt)
. This is simply the duration of the interval, calculated as the final time minus the initial time (
t_final − t_initial
).¹⁶
Step 4: Calculate Acceleration
. Divide the change in velocity from Step 2 by the time taken from Step 3:
a = Δv / Δt
.¹⁶
Worked Example:
Consider a data table for a moving object:
Calculate the acceleration between
t=1 s
and
t=3 s
Interval
: The interval is from
t=1 s
to
t=3 s
Change in Velocity (Δv)
Initial velocity (
u
) at
t=1 s
is 4 m/s.
Final velocity (
v
) at
t=3 s
is 12 m/s.
Δv = 12 m/s − 4 m/s = 8 m/s
Time Taken (Δt)
Δt = 3 s − 1 s = 2 s
Calculate Acceleration (a)
a = Δv / Δt = 8 m/s / 2 s = 4 m/s²
By performing this calculation for different intervals, one can determine if the acceleration is constant. For instance, calculating the acceleration between
t=0 s
and
t=2 s
also yields
4 m/s²
, indicating constant acceleration in the first three seconds. However, between
t=3 s
and
t=4 s
, the change in velocity is zero, so the acceleration is
0 m/s²
Section 2: The Speed-Time Graph as an Analytical Tool

The speed-time graph is the primary visual method for analyzing the motion of an object. Its geometric properties, particularly its gradient, correspond directly to physical quantities, providing a powerful way to understand acceleration.
2.1 Constructing and Interpreting a Speed-Time Graph
A speed-time graph plots the speed (or velocity in one dimension) of an object against time. By convention:
The
vertical axis (y-axis)
represents speed, typically in metres per second (m/s).
The
horizontal axis (x-axis)
represents time, typically in seconds (s).¹⁷
The resulting line or curve on the graph provides a visual narrative of how the object's speed has changed over the duration of its journey.¹⁹
2.2 The Gradient: The Key to Understanding Acceleration
The most critical feature of a speed-time graph is its
gradient
(or slope), which represents the
acceleration
of the object.²⁰ This relationship is not a coincidence but a direct mathematical equivalence. The reasoning is as follows:
The mathematical formula for the gradient of a line is the "rise" divided by the "run," or the change in the y-axis value divided by the change in the x-axis value:
Gradient = Δy / Δx
On a speed-time graph, the y-axis represents speed (velocity,
v
) and the x-axis represents time (
t
Substituting these physical quantities into the gradient formula gives:
Gradient = Δv / Δt
This expression,
Δv / Δt
, is the very definition of acceleration (
a
Therefore, the physical quantity of acceleration is mathematically identical to the geometric property of the gradient on a speed-time graph:
a = gradient
This fundamental connection underpins all graphical analysis of motion and allows one to determine acceleration simply by analyzing the shape and steepness of the graph's line.²²
2.3 Interpreting the Gradient's Characteristics
The specific characteristics of the gradient provide detailed information about the object's acceleration:
Positive Gradient (Upward Slope)
: This indicates that the speed is increasing. It represents a
positive acceleration
.²¹
Negative Gradient (Downward Slope)
: This indicates that the speed is decreasing. It represents a
negative acceleration
, or deceleration.²¹
Zero Gradient (Horizontal Line)
: This indicates that the speed is not changing. It represents
zero acceleration
, meaning the object is moving at a constant speed.²⁰
Steepness of the Gradient
: The magnitude of the gradient reveals the magnitude of the acceleration. A
steeper slope
(whether positive or negative) signifies a
larger acceleration
or deceleration, meaning the speed is changing rapidly. A
gentler, shallower slope
signifies a
smaller acceleration
, meaning the speed is changing more gradually.²⁵
Section 3: Identifying Constant Acceleration on a Speed-Time Graph

Constant, or uniform, acceleration is the simplest type of accelerated motion. It is characterized by the velocity changing by an equal amount in every equal time period.⁴ On a speed-time graph, this uniformity is represented by
straight lines
3.1 The Signature of Constancy: The Straight Line
A straight line on any graph has a gradient that is constant and unchanging along its length.²⁶ Since the gradient of a speed-time graph represents acceleration, a
straight line on a speed-time graph signifies that the object is moving with constant acceleration
.²³ The motion can be broken down into three distinct cases.
3.2 Case 1: Constant Positive Acceleration
Appearance
: An upward-sloping straight line.²³
Interpretation
: The object's speed is increasing at a steady, constant rate. For every second that passes, the speed increases by the same amount.
Diagram
: A graph showing a straight line starting from the origin (representing acceleration from rest) or from a positive y-intercept (representing acceleration from an initial speed) and rising linearly.
Worked Example
: A car accelerates from 0 m/s to 15 m/s in 10 seconds. Its speed-time graph is a straight line from (0, 0) to (10, 15). The acceleration is the gradient:
This constant value of 1.5 m/s² indicates that the car's speed increases by 1.5 m/s every second.¹⁹
3.3 Case 2: Constant Negative Acceleration (Deceleration)
Appearance
: A downward-sloping straight line.²³
Interpretation
: The object's speed is decreasing at a steady, constant rate. It is slowing down uniformly.
Diagram
: A graph showing a straight line starting from an initial speed and descending linearly, either to a lower speed or to the x-axis (representing the object coming to rest).
Worked Example
: A vehicle travelling at 25 m/s applies its brakes and comes to a stop in 20 seconds. Its speed-time graph is a straight line from (0, 25) to (20, 0). The acceleration is the gradient:
The negative sign indicates that the acceleration is in the opposite direction to the velocity, causing the object to slow down. This is a constant deceleration of 1.25 m/s².¹⁹
3.4 Case 3: Zero Acceleration (Constant Velocity)
Appearance
: A horizontal straight line (a line with a gradient of zero).²⁰
Interpretation

: The object's speed is not changing over time; it is moving at a constant velocity. A special case is a horizontal line along the x-axis (where speed = 0), which signifies that the object is stationary.²⁰
Diagram
: A graph showing a horizontal line at a non-zero speed value.
Worked Example
: An object moves at a constant speed of 15 m/s for 10 seconds. The change in velocity (Δv) over this period is
. The acceleration is therefore:
a = Δv / Δt = 0 m/s / 10 s = 0 m/s²
This confirms that a horizontal line corresponds to zero acceleration.
Section 4: Identifying Changing Acceleration on a Speed-Time Graph
When an object's acceleration is not uniform, its motion is more complex. This scenario of non-uniform or changing acceleration is represented on a speed-time graph by
curved lines
. This is a key concept for higher-tier iGCSE students.
4.1 The Signature of Change: The Curve
A curved line on a speed-time graph has a gradient that is continuously changing at every point along its path.²⁶ Since the gradient represents acceleration, a
curved line is the definitive signature of an object moving with changing acceleration
.²⁶ The specific shape of the curve reveals how the acceleration is changing.
4.2 Case 1: Increasing Positive Acceleration
Appearance
: An upward-curving line that becomes progressively
steeper
.²⁶
Interpretation

: The object is speeding up, and the rate at which it speeds up is also increasing. The gradient is positive and its value is increasing. This means the speed changes by the same amount in increasingly shorter intervals of time.²⁶
Diagram
: A graph showing a curve that starts shallowly and bends upwards more sharply as time progresses, as illustrated in reference.²⁶
4.3 Case 2: Decreasing Positive Acceleration
Appearance
: An upward-curving line that becomes progressively
shallower
or flatter.²⁶
Interpretation

: The object is still speeding up (the gradient is still positive), but the rate at which it is speeding up is decreasing. The gradient is positive but its value is decreasing, approaching zero. The speed changes by the same amount in increasingly longer intervals of time.²⁶ A real-world example is a car accelerating towards its top speed; the initial acceleration is high, but it lessens as air resistance increases.³⁰
Diagram
: A graph showing a curve that starts steeply and bends over to become more horizontal as time progresses, as illustrated in reference.²⁶
4.4 Case 3: Changing Negative Acceleration (Deceleration)
Appearance
: A downward-curving line. The curve can become shallower (less steep) or steeper.
Interpretation (Decreasing Deceleration)

: A downward curve that becomes shallower indicates that the object is slowing down, but the rate of slowing is decreasing. The gradient is negative but is becoming less negative (approaching zero). An example is an object falling with air resistance that is approaching its terminal velocity.²⁶
Diagram
: A graph showing a curve that starts with a steep negative slope and flattens out towards a horizontal line, as illustrated in reference.²⁶
4.5 Determining Instantaneous Acceleration: The Tangent Method
For a curved speed-time graph, the acceleration is different at every point. Using the formula
a = Δv / Δt
between two points on the curve will only yield the
average
acceleration over that time interval. To find the acceleration at a specific moment in time—the
instantaneous acceleration
—a different technique is required.
The graphical method for finding the gradient at a single point on a curve is to draw a
tangent

at that point.²⁶ A tangent is a straight line that "just touches" the curve at the desired point without crossing it, matching the curve's gradient at that exact location.³¹ By calculating the gradient of this straight tangent line, one can determine the instantaneous acceleration at that precise moment.
Procedure
Identify the point on the curve where the instantaneous acceleration is required.
Place a ruler on the graph so that it just touches the curve at that single point. Adjust the angle of the ruler until it appears to follow the direction of the curve at that point.
Draw a long, straight line for the tangent. A longer line allows for a more accurate gradient calculation.
Choose two points that are far apart on the tangent line and form a large "rise over run" triangle.

Calculate the gradient of the tangent using these two points. The result is the instantaneous acceleration at the chosen moment.²⁶ Examiners often award credit for the clear drawing of a large gradient triangle on the graph.²⁵
