rt.x: 4.2 Key Factors Affecting Field Strength: A Comprehensive Summary
The ability to control the strength of a magnetic field produced by a current is essential for its practical applications. The strength of the field can be altered by several factors:
For Both Straight Wires and Solenoids:
Current Magnitude (I)
: The magnetic field strength is directly proportional to the current. Increasing the current increases the field strength.¹⁶
Specific to Solenoids:
Number of Turns (N)
: The more turns of wire a solenoid has, the stronger its magnetic field will be, as the fields from each turn add together.²¹
Coil Length (L)

: The concentration of the turns is also important. A shorter solenoid with the same number of turns will have a stronger magnetic field because the turns are more densely packed. Therefore, the field strength is proportional to the
number of turns per unit length (N/L)
.²¹
Core Material
: The material inside the coil has a dramatic effect on the field strength. While a solenoid with an air core produces a magnetic field, inserting a core made of a soft magnetic material, such as
soft iron
, will increase the strength of the magnetic field significantly.⁵ Such a device is called an
electromagnet

The role of the iron core is not merely passive; it acts as a magnetic amplifier. The initial magnetic field produced by the current in the solenoid causes the microscopic magnetic regions (domains) within the iron to align with the external field.²⁹ This process, known as induced magnetism, turns the iron core into a powerful temporary magnet itself. The magnetic field of the aligned iron core then adds to the original field of the solenoid, resulting in a total magnetic field that is many times stronger than that of the solenoid alone.²⁰
4.3 Common Misconceptions and Examiner Guidance
To achieve success in examinations, it is vital to use precise language and avoid common errors.
Right-Hand Grip Rule Application

: Students must be clear that there are two distinct applications of the rule. For a straight wire, the thumb follows the current. For a solenoid, the fingers follow the current.²⁴ Confusing these two applications is a frequent mistake.
Terminology for Coils

: When describing how to increase the strength of a solenoid, it is more precise to state "increase the number of turns on the coil" rather than the ambiguous "add more coils." The term "coil" refers to the entire solenoid object.²¹
Conventional Current
: It is worth reiterating that all direction-finding rules in this topic rely on the direction of conventional current (positive to negative), not electron flow.
Conclusion

The magnetic effect of an electric current is a fundamental principle of physics that demonstrates the deep connection between electricity and magnetism. The flow of current in a conductor, whether a straight wire or a coiled solenoid, generates a predictable magnetic field. The characteristics of this field are determined by the geometry of the conductor and the properties of the current.
For a
straight wire
, the field consists of concentric circles with no poles. Its direction is found using the Right-Hand Grip Rule, where the thumb follows the current.
For a
solenoid

, the field is strong and uniform internally and resembles that of a bar magnet externally, with distinct North and South poles. Its polarity is found using an adapted Right-Hand Grip Rule, where the fingers follow the current.
In both configurations, two key relationships hold true:
Changing the magnitude of the current directly changes the strength of the magnetic field.
A larger current produces a stronger field.
Changing the direction of the current reverses the orientation of the magnetic field.
For a wire, this reverses the circular direction of the field lines; for a solenoid, it reverses the polarity, swapping the North and South poles.

These principles are not merely theoretical; they are the operational basis for countless technologies that power and shape the modern world. A clear understanding of these cause-and-effect relationships is essential for any student of physics.

PE4.32.title: Motor Effect: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field

rt.x: The Genesis of the Force — A Tale of Two Interacting Fields
The phenomenon where a conductor carrying an electric current experiences a force when placed in a magnetic field is a cornerstone of electromagnetism, known as the
motor effect

.¹ This effect is not a magical or instantaneous action but the result of a direct, physical interaction between two distinct magnetic fields: one created by the current in the conductor itself, and the other being the external magnetic field in which the conductor is situated. Understanding the origin and nature of these two fields is the first step toward comprehending why this force exists.
The First Field: The Conductor's Own Magnetism

A fundamental principle, first demonstrated by Hans Christian Ørsted, is that any moving electric charge generates a magnetic field.³ Since an electric current is defined as the rate of flow of charge, it follows that any conductor carrying a current is surrounded by its own magnetic field.⁶ For a long, straight conductor, this magnetic field takes a specific and predictable shape: a series of
concentric circles
centered on the wire.⁶ These circular field lines lie in a plane that is perpendicular to the direction of the current flow.¹⁰
To determine the direction of this magnetic field, a simple yet powerful mnemonic known as the
Right-Hand Grip Rule
is used.¹² The rule is applied as follows:
Imagine gripping the wire with your right hand.
Point your thumb in the direction of the
conventional current
. It is critical to note that conventional current is defined as flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the power source.⁶
The direction in which your fingers curl around the wire indicates the direction of the magnetic field lines.³
For example, if a vertical wire carries an upward current, the Right-Hand Grip Rule shows that the magnetic field lines will circulate in an
anticlockwise
direction when viewed from above.⁶ This self-generated magnetic field is the first of the two key players in the motor effect.
The Second Field: The External Environment
The second component required for the motor effect is an
external magnetic field

. This field is typically produced by permanent magnets, such as a large horseshoe magnet, or by another current-carrying coil, known as an electromagnet.² In the context of demonstrating the motor effect, this external field is usually designed to be
uniform

in the region where the conductor is placed. A uniform magnetic field is one where the field has the same strength and direction at all points. It is visually represented by a series of parallel, evenly spaced magnetic field lines.¹⁹ By convention, these external magnetic field lines always originate from a
North pole
and terminate on a
South pole
.²
The Interaction: Where Force is Born

The force of the motor effect arises when the circular magnetic field of the current-carrying conductor is superimposed upon the uniform external magnetic field.² The two fields must interact and merge, as magnetic field lines
cannot cross
one another.²³ This interaction creates a distortion in the overall magnetic field pattern surrounding the conductor.
On one side of the conductor, the direction of its circular field lines will be the
same
as the direction of the external field lines. In this region, the fields reinforce each other, resulting in a
stronger, more concentrated magnetic field
. The field lines become bunched together, indicating a region of high magnetic field density.¹⁸
On the opposite side of the conductor, its circular field lines are directed
opposite
to the external field lines. Here, the fields partially cancel each other out, creating a
weaker, less concentrated magnetic field
. The field lines are spread further apart, indicating a region of low magnetic field density.¹⁸

This imbalance in the magnetic field strength around the conductor creates a net force. The conductor experiences a "push" from the region of the stronger, denser magnetic field towards the region of the weaker, less dense field.¹⁸ This can be conceptualized as a difference in magnetic pressure, with the conductor being moved from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure. This force is the tangible manifestation of the motor effect.
This interaction is also governed by
Newton's Third Law of Motion

. The force is mutual: just as the external magnet exerts a force on the wire, the wire's magnetic field exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnet.²⁰ In most experimental setups, the conductor is the object with less inertia and is free to move, so it is the one observed to accelerate. However, the underlying physics is a symmetrical interaction between two magnetic objects.
Predicting the Direction of Force — Mastering Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
While the field interaction model provides a deep conceptual understanding of why the force exists, a more direct and practical tool is needed to quickly determine its direction. This tool is
Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
, a mnemonic developed by the English physicist John Ambrose Fleming in the late 19th century specifically for analyzing electric motors.²³
Introduction to the Rule
Fleming's Left-Hand Rule provides a simple method for relating the directions of three mutually perpendicular quantities: the
Force
on the conductor, the external
Magnetic Field
, and the electric
Current

flowing through the conductor.² It is a physical embodiment of the underlying vector relationship that governs electromagnetism, making complex three-dimensional problems accessible and intuitive.²⁷ The rule is specifically for
motors

, where an input of current and a magnetic field produces an output of force and motion. This is distinct from Fleming's Right-Hand Rule, which applies to generators where an input of motion in a field produces a current.²³
A Step-by-Step Guide to Application
To apply the rule correctly, the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger of the
left hand
must be held at right angles (90 degrees) to each other, representing three orthogonal axes.²⁸ Each digit corresponds to a specific physical quantity, which can be remembered using the mnemonic
FBI
Thumb
: Represents the direction of the
Thrust
or
F
orce (F).
Forefinger
: Represents the direction of the Magnetic
F
ield (B), from North to South.
Second (Middle) Finger
: Represents the direction of the Conventional
C
urrent (I), from positive to negative.
To solve a problem, one should orient the hand in a systematic sequence:
Align the Forefinger with the Field
: Point your forefinger in the direction of the external magnetic field, from the North pole to the South pole.²¹
Align the Middle Finger with the Current
: Without changing the direction of your forefinger, rotate your wrist until your middle finger points in the direction of the conventional current flow in the wire.²
Read the Direction of the Force
: Your thumb will now automatically point in the direction of the force that the conductor will experience.²

The structure of the rule itself reflects the optimal conditions for the motor effect. The mutually perpendicular arrangement of the fingers corresponds to the physical condition where the force on the conductor is at its
maximum
: when the current flows at a 90-degree angle to the magnetic field lines.¹⁸ If the current were parallel to the magnetic field, there would be no interaction and
no force
, a scenario where the rule cannot be meaningfully applied.²
Handling 3D Scenarios
In diagrams, it is often necessary to represent directions that are perpendicular to the plane of the page. A standard convention is used for this purpose ³⁴:
A circle with a dot in the center (
) represents a vector pointing
out of the page
, towards the observer. This can be visualized as the tip of an arrow approaching.
A circle with a cross in the center (
) represents a vector pointing
into the page
, away from the observer. This can be visualized as the tail feathers of an arrow moving away.

For instance, consider a wire placed in a magnetic field that runs from left to right. If the current in the wire is flowing into the page (⊗), applying Fleming's Left-Hand Rule would proceed as follows:
Field
: Point the forefinger to the right.
Current
: Rotate the hand so the middle finger points into the page.
Force
: The thumb now points
downwards
Therefore, the wire would experience a downward force.²
A Systematic Analysis of Reversal Effects

The core of the iGCSE syllabus objective is to understand how the direction of the force is affected by changes to the system's inputs. A systematic analysis reveals a clear and predictable set of rules that are fundamental to the control of all electric motors.
The Consequence of Reversing the Current
If the direction of the current flowing through the conductor is reversed, while the direction of the external magnetic field is held constant, the direction of the
force on the conductor will also be reversed
.²⁶
This outcome can be understood through both of the models previously discussed:
Field Interaction Model

: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the wire's own magnetic field, according to the Right-Hand Grip Rule. This causes the regions of field reinforcement and cancellation to swap sides. The area that was previously a high-density field becomes a low-density field, and vice versa. Consequently, the direction of the "push" from high to low magnetic pressure is inverted, and the force acts in the opposite direction.¹⁸
Fleming's Left-Hand Rule Verification

: Applying the rule demonstrates this effect plainly. If the forefinger (Field) is held in a fixed direction and the middle finger (Current) is rotated 180 degrees to point in the opposite direction, the thumb (Force) must also point in the opposite direction to maintain the mutually perpendicular relationship.³⁰
The Consequence of Reversing the Magnetic Field

Similarly, if the direction of the external magnetic field is reversed (for example, by swapping the physical positions of the North and South poles of the magnets), while the direction of the current is held constant, the direction of the
force on the conductor will also be reversed
.²⁶
Field Interaction Model

: Reversing the external field again causes the regions of reinforcement and cancellation to swap sides relative to the conductor. The side where the two fields were previously aligned is now in opposition, and vice versa. This inverts the magnetic pressure gradient and reverses the resulting force.
Fleming's Left-Hand Rule Verification

: If the middle finger (Current) is held in a fixed direction and the forefinger (Field) is pointed in the opposite direction, the thumb (Force) must reverse its direction to preserve the geometry of the rule.³⁹

The fact that reversing either the current or the field produces the same outcome—a reversal of the force—reveals a fundamental symmetry in the motor effect. The current and the magnetic field are equal partners in generating the force, and a change in the direction of either one has an equivalent impact on the direction of the output force. This understanding is crucial for engineering control systems. The ability to precisely control the direction of motion by simply reversing the flow of current is the principle that allows electric motors to operate bidirectionally, a vital feature in applications from robotics to electric vehicles.⁴⁰
The Nullifying Effect of a Double Reversal
A key test of understanding is to consider what happens when
both the current and the magnetic field are reversed simultaneously
. In this scenario, the two reversals cancel each other out, and the force acts in its
original, unchanged direction
.³⁹

This can be verified with Fleming's Left-Hand Rule. If one starts in a baseline position and then reverses the direction of the forefinger (Field) and also reverses the direction of the middle finger (Current), the thumb (Force) will end up pointing in the same direction it was at the beginning. Each reversal introduces a 180-degree flip to the force vector; two such flips return it to its initial state.
The relationships can be summarized for clarity:
Experimental Verification and Factors of Influence

The principles of the motor effect and the consequences of reversal are not merely theoretical constructs; they are readily observable and verifiable through straightforward laboratory experiments, as required by the iGCSE syllabus.⁴¹
Designing the Experiment
A classic apparatus for demonstrating the motor effect qualitatively consists of the following components ⁴¹:
Power Supply
: A low-voltage direct current (d.c.) power source.
Conductor

: A lightweight, movable conductor. A common choice is a short aluminum or copper rod designed to rest across two parallel, bare copper wires that act as rails. Alternatively, a single wire can be suspended between the poles of a magnet so that it is free to swing.
Magnetic Field
: A strong, uniform magnetic field, typically provided by a large horseshoe magnet placed so the conductor sits between its poles.
Circuit Components

: Connecting wires, a switch to complete the circuit, an ammeter to monitor the current, and a variable resistor (rheostat) to control the magnitude of the current. A reversing switch is also essential for investigating the reversal effects.
Conducting the Investigation
The experiment is conducted in a series of logical steps to verify the core principles:
Observing the Force

: The circuit is assembled with the conductor placed within the magnetic field, perpendicular to the field lines. When the switch is closed, current flows through the conductor, which is immediately observed to move (e.g., the rod rolls along the rails or the suspended wire swings out of its resting position).¹⁸ This provides direct evidence that a force acts on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.
Verifying Reversal of Current

: The direction of the conductor's motion is noted. The reversing switch is then used to reverse the polarity of the power supply, causing the current to flow in the opposite direction. Upon closing the switch again, the conductor is observed to move in the exact opposite direction to the initial observation.²² This confirms that reversing the current reverses the force.
Verifying Reversal of Field

: The circuit is returned to its original configuration. The permanent magnet is then physically inverted, swapping the positions of its North and South poles and thus reversing the direction of the magnetic field. When the switch is closed, the conductor is again observed to move in the opposite direction to the initial observation.³⁰ This confirms that reversing the magnetic field also reverses the force.
Factors Affecting the Magnitude of the Force

While the primary focus of the syllabus point is on the direction of the force, a complete understanding of the motor effect involves knowing the factors that influence its strength or magnitude. These factors are directly relevant to the operation of d.c. motors and can be investigated with the same experimental apparatus.⁴² The magnitude of the force is increased by:
Increasing the Current (I)

: Using the variable resistor to allow a larger current to flow through the conductor results in a visibly larger and more rapid acceleration. This is because a greater current produces a stronger magnetic field around the wire, leading to a more powerful interaction with the external field.²
Increasing the Strength of the External Magnetic Field (B)
: Replacing the magnet with a stronger one (one with a higher magnetic flux density) also results in a greater force on the conductor.²
Increasing the Length of the Conductor in the Field (L)

: Using a longer conductor, or arranging the apparatus so that a greater length of the existing conductor is inside the magnetic field, increases the total force. This is because the force acts on every moving charge within the field, so a longer wire contains more charges to be acted upon.²

These qualitative observations from the experiment form the basis of the quantitative relationship for the force, which at a higher level is expressed by the formula F=IlBsinθ.³³ This shows how scientific inquiry progresses from observing a phenomenon to identifying the variables that control it, and finally to formulating a mathematical law to describe it precisely.
From Principle to Practice — The Direct Current (D.C.) Motor
The culmination of all these principles—the existence of the force, the rules governing its direction, and the factors affecting its magnitude—is found in the operation of the
direct current (d.c.) motor
. A d.c. motor is a device that brilliantly harnesses the motor effect to convert electrical energy into useful mechanical kinetic energy in the form of continuous rotation.⁴²
From a Single Wire to a Rotating Coil
A practical motor enhances the turning effect by replacing a single straight wire with a
rectangular coil

, often with many turns of wire.¹⁸ This coil is mounted on an axle and placed within a strong magnetic field. When current flows through the coil, the two sides parallel to the axle are perpendicular to the magnetic field. Applying Fleming's Left-Hand Rule reveals the key to its operation:
On one side of the coil, the current flows in one direction (e.g., away from the viewer). This produces a force in one direction (e.g.,
upwards
).³⁵
On the opposite side of the coil, the current is flowing in the reverse direction (e.g., towards the viewer). This produces a force in the opposite direction (e.g.,
downwards
).³⁵
This pair of equal and opposite forces acting on the sides of the coil creates a turning effect, known as a
torque
, which causes the coil to rotate about its axle.⁴²
The Problem of Continuous Rotation and its Solution

If the current were to flow in the same direction around the coil continuously, the motor would not work. After rotating 180 degrees, the side that was initially pushed up would now be on the other side of the motor, where the force would still be directed upwards. This would oppose the rotation and try to turn the coil back. The motor would simply oscillate back and forth or get stuck in a vertical position where the forces pull outwards but provide no turning effect.¹⁸
To solve this, a crucial component is introduced: the
split-ring commutator
.³⁷ This is a metal ring, connected to the ends of the coil, that has been split into two electrically separate halves. Two stationary carbon blocks, called
brushes
, press against the rotating commutator, delivering current from the power supply to the coil.

The function of the split-ring commutator is to act as an automatic, mechanically timed reversing switch. Every half-rotation (180 degrees), as the coil passes the vertical position, the momentum of the coil carries it slightly forward. At this point, each brush slides from one half of the commutator to the other. This action ingeniously
reverses the direction of the current
flowing into the coil relative to the coil itself.³⁷
A Symphony of Reversals for Continuous Motion

This periodic reversal of the current is the key to continuous rotation. By reversing the current in the coil precisely every half turn, the direction of the forces on each side of the coil is also reversed, in perfect accordance with the principle that reversing the current reverses the force.

This ensures that the side of the coil that is moving up always experiences an upward force, and the side that is moving down always experiences a downward force, regardless of which side of the motor they are on. The torque, therefore, consistently acts in the same rotational direction, driving the motor in a smooth, continuous spin.³⁷ The d.c. motor is thus a masterful application of the reversal principles, using a simple yet brilliant mechanical switch to turn a fundamental physical effect into one of the most important inventions in modern technology.

This elegant interplay also highlights the profound symmetry in electromagnetism. The motor effect uses a field and current to create motion (Force = Field + Current). The reverse is also true: moving a conductor in a magnetic field will induce a current (Current = Field + Force), a principle known as
electromagnetic induction
, which is the basis of the electric generator.³⁶ These two effects are two sides of the same fundamental interaction, demonstrating the deep and interconnected nature of electricity and magnetism.

Introduction: From Invisible Fields to Tangible Force

The direct current (d.c.) motor stands as a cornerstone of modern technology, a device that elegantly transforms electrical energy into the mechanical motion that powers countless aspects of our daily lives.¹ From the vibration of a mobile phone and the spinning turntable in a microwave to the electric windows in a car and the complex movements of robotic arms, the d.c. motor is an often unseen yet indispensable workhorse.³ At its core, the d.c. motor is the quintessential application of one of the most fundamental principles in physics: the profound and inseparable link between electricity and magnetism.¹ This report seeks to deconstruct this remarkable device, providing a comprehensive analysis aligned with the IGCSE Physics curriculum. It will explore the phenomenon of the turning effect experienced by a current-carrying coil within a magnetic field and meticulously analyze the three key factors that govern its magnitude: the number of turns on the coil, the current flowing through it, and the strength of the magnetic field.⁶
Section 1: The Fundamental Interaction - The Motor Effect

The operation of every d.c. motor is predicated on a principle known as the "motor effect." This phenomenon describes how a conductor carrying an electric current experiences a physical force when it is placed within an external magnetic field.¹ This force is not an abstract concept but a tangible push or pull that arises from a fundamental interaction between two distinct magnetic fields.
The Two Interacting Fields
To understand the origin of this force, it is essential to recognize that two magnetic fields are at play:
The External Magnetic Field

: In a simple motor, this is a static magnetic field, typically produced by permanent magnets that form the stationary part of the motor, known as the stator. This field is characterized by magnetic field lines that emanate from a north pole and enter a south pole.⁹
The Conductor's Magnetic Field

: A foundational principle of electromagnetism, discovered by Hans Christian Ørsted, is that any wire carrying an electric current generates its own magnetic field.⁵ For a straight conductor, this field takes the form of concentric circles around the wire, with its direction determined by the Right-Hand Grip Rule.
The Mechanism of Force Generation

The motor effect is the result of the superposition, or interaction, of these two magnetic fields.⁸ On one side of the current-carrying wire, the circular magnetic field it generates will be in the same direction as the external field from the permanent magnets. Here, the fields reinforce each other, creating a region of a stronger, more concentrated magnetic field. On the opposite side of the wire, the conductor's field opposes the external field. Here, the fields partially cancel, creating a region of a weaker magnetic field. This imbalance in field strength around the conductor creates a net force, pushing the wire from the region of the stronger field toward the region of the weaker field.¹⁴ This provides a clear physical mechanism for the force: it is a consequence of the distortion of the magnetic field caused by the presence of the current-carrying wire.
The underlying law governing this interaction is the Lorentz force.¹ While a full vector analysis is complex, the magnitude of the force (F) can be expressed by the formula:
F=IlBsinθ

where I is the current, l is the length of the conductor within the field, B is the magnetic field strength, and θ is the angle between the conductor and the magnetic field lines.⁸ This equation is fundamental as it establishes the direct proportionality between the force and the key variables of current (I) and magnetic field strength (B), which will be explored in Section 5.
Section 2: Predicting the Direction of Motion - A Masterclass in Fleming's Left-Hand Rule

While the formula for the motor effect quantifies the magnitude of the force, a different tool is needed to predict its direction. This tool is Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, a powerful and reliable mnemonic developed in the late 19th century by English electrical engineer John Ambrose Fleming.⁷ It provides a simple method for determining the direction of the force (or motion) when the directions of the magnetic field and the electric current are known.

A critical aspect of the motor effect is that the force, the magnetic field, and the current are all mutually perpendicular to one another.⁹ This orthogonal relationship means they exist at 90-degree angles to each other, which is why in two-dimensional diagrams, the force is often depicted as acting "into the page" or "out of the page."
Step-by-Step Application Guide

To apply the rule correctly, one must use their left hand and orient the thumb, forefinger, and middle finger so that they are all perpendicular to each other.¹⁸ Each digit is then assigned a specific physical quantity:
Forefinger (or First finger)
: Represents the direction of the magnetic
F
ield. This finger should always point from the North pole to the South pole of the external magnets.⁹
Centre finger (or seCond finger)
: Represents the direction of the
C
urrent. This finger should point in the direction of conventional current, which flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the power source.¹⁴
Thumb
: Represents the direction of the resulting
Th
rust or
M
otion. The thumb will point in the direction of the force exerted on the conductor.⁷

To aid memorization, several mnemonics have been developed. One popular method uses the acronym FBI, corresponding to Force (Thumb), Field (First finger), and Current (Centre finger, using 'I' as the symbol for current).¹⁴ Another vivid analogy involves pretending the hand is a gun: you "Fire the Field" with the index finger, "Feel the Force" of the recoil with the thumb, and "Kill the Current" with the middle finger.¹⁴

It is crucial to distinguish this rule from its counterpart, Fleming's Right-Hand Rule. The Left-Hand Rule is used for motors, where an electric current is the input that causes motion. The Right-Hand Rule is used for generators, where motion is the input that induces an electric current.¹⁴

rt.x: Section 3: From a Simple Push to a Continuous Turn - The Genesis of Torque in a Coil

A linear force on a single wire is useful, but the primary function of a motor is to produce continuous rotation. This is achieved by moving from a single straight conductor to a rectangular coil of wire.²⁰ The geometry of the coil is a deliberate engineering design that masterfully converts the linear motor effect into a rotational turning effect.

When a rectangular coil is placed in a magnetic field and a current is passed through it, the forces on the different sides of the coil must be analyzed separately. The two sides of the coil that run parallel to the direction of the magnetic field experience little to no force, as the angle θ between the current and the field is zero or 180 degrees, making sinθ=0.²²

However, the two sides of the coil that cut perpendicularly across the magnetic field lines are where the crucial action occurs. Because the current flows into one side of the coil and out the other, the direction of current in these two opposite sides is reversed relative to each other. Applying Fleming's Left-Hand Rule to each of these sides reveals that the force on one side is directed upwards, while the force on the other side is directed downwards.¹²
This pair of forces is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Crucially, they are not collinear—they do not act along the same line. Such a pair of forces is known as a
couple
.²⁰ A couple produces a turning effect, or
torque

, which causes the coil to rotate about its central axis.²² While the net linear force on the coil as a whole is zero (it does not move up, down, left, or right), the net torque is non-zero, resulting in pure rotation.²² This is the genesis of the turning effect in a d.c. motor.
Section 4: The Ingenuity of Continuous Rotation - The Split-Ring Commutator

The creation of torque via a couple is a major step, but it does not guarantee continuous rotation. If the coil were connected directly to a d.c. supply, it would rotate for a half-turn and then stop. As the coil passes the vertical position, the direction of the torque would reverse, pushing it back to where it started. The motor would simply oscillate back and forth and become stuck.¹⁵
The solution to this problem is an ingenious device called the
split-ring commutator
. This component is a metal ring, split into two electrically insulated halves, which is mounted on the motor's axle and rotates along with the coil.²⁴ Stationary blocks of carbon, known as
brushes

, are held by springs to press against the rotating commutator segments. These brushes deliver the electric current from the d.c. power supply to the coil.²⁴ Carbon is an ideal material as it is a good conductor of electricity but is also soft and self-lubricating, minimizing wear on the copper commutator segments.²⁶
The commutator's function is best understood by following one complete rotation:
Horizontal Position (Maximum Torque)

: Current flows from a brush into one commutator segment, through the coil, and out through the other segment and brush. The forces create a couple that produces a strong turning effect, for example, in a clockwise direction.²⁵
Vertical Position (Zero Torque)

: As the coil rotates towards the vertical position, the brushes are about to cross the insulating gaps between the commutator segments. At the exact vertical point, the brushes briefly lose contact with the commutator segments. The electrical circuit is broken, no current flows, and the electromagnetic force on the coil drops to zero.²⁵ This is not a design flaw but a critical feature. At this orientation, any force would be non-turning and would oppose further rotation.
Past the Vertical Position

: The coil's own momentum carries it past this vertical 'dead spot'.²⁵ As it does so, the commutator segments make contact with the opposite brushes from which they started. The segment that was connected to the positive brush is now connected to the negative brush, and vice versa.
Current Reversal
: This swapping of connections reverses the direction of the current within the rotating coil itself.²⁴
Continuous Torque

: Although the sides of the coil have physically moved to the opposite side of the motor, the reversed current ensures that the forces on them continue to produce a torque in the original direction (still clockwise). The side of the coil that is now on the left experiences an upward force, and the side on the right experiences a downward force, sustaining the rotation.²⁵

This cycle repeats every half-turn. The split-ring commutator acts as a perfectly timed, automatic mechanical switch. It intelligently manages the application of force by reversing the current precisely when needed, ensuring the torque always acts in the same direction to produce smooth, continuous rotation.¹
Section 5: Amplifying the Effect - A Detailed Examination of the Key Factors

The turning effect, or torque, of a d.c. motor is not a fixed quantity. Its magnitude can be precisely controlled to make a motor more powerful, allowing it to turn faster or drive a heavier load. The three primary factors that increase the magnitude of this turning effect are the number of turns on the coil, the size of the current, and the strength of the magnetic field.⁶
(a) Increasing the Number of Turns on the Coil

A practical motor armature does not consist of a single loop of wire but rather a coil made of many turns wrapped together.⁵ Each turn of wire within the coil carries the current through the magnetic field and experiences the motor effect. The total force on one side of the coil is the sum of the individual forces acting on each wire segment. Therefore, a coil with 'N' turns will experience approximately 'N' times the force—and thus 'N' times the torque—of a single loop, assuming all other factors remain constant.⁵ This acts as a simple but highly effective force-multiplying mechanism.
(b) Increasing the Current

The magnitude of the force on the coil is directly proportional to the electric current flowing through it.⁸ If the current is doubled, the turning force will also double. The physical justification for this lies in the interaction of the magnetic fields. A larger current signifies a greater rate of flow of charge, which in turn generates a stronger magnetic field around the wires of the coil.⁵ This more powerful magnetic field interacts more forcefully with the static field of the permanent magnets, resulting in a greater repulsive and attractive force on the sides of the coil and, consequently, a larger torque.¹²
(c) Increasing the Strength of the Magnetic Field

The turning force is also directly proportional to the strength of the external magnetic field, often denoted by the symbol B.⁸ A stronger magnetic field is one where the magnetic field lines are more densely packed. When the current-carrying coil is placed in this denser field, its own magnetic field interacts with a greater concentration of external field lines. This more intense interaction produces a larger force on the wires of the coil, leading to a greater turning effect.¹² In practice, this can be achieved by using more powerful permanent magnets or, in larger and more powerful motors, by replacing the permanent magnets with strong electromagnets.¹⁰

rt.x: From the moment our day begins, our lives are supported by the silent, efficient operation of d.c. motors.⁴ Their versatility, precise speed control, and high starting torque make them suitable for an astonishingly wide range of applications across every sector of society.
Household Appliances

: The modern home is powered by dozens of d.c. motors. They are found in electric toothbrushes, cooling fans, blenders, and the compressors of refrigerators. They spin the drum in washing machines, rotate the turntable in microwaves, and drive the powerful suction in vacuum cleaners.³
Automotive Systems
: The average car contains numerous d.c. motors. They power electric windows, windshield wipers, fuel pumps, adjustable seats, and the fans for the engine cooling and cabin HVAC systems.³²
Consumer Electronics and Toys

: D.c. motors are integral to consumer electronics. They spin the disks in optical drives, provide the lift for drones, power remote-controlled cars, create the vibration in gaming controllers, and operate the focusing and zoom mechanisms in digital cameras.³³
Industrial and Robotics

: In industrial settings, d.c. motors drive conveyor belts, power the precise joints of robotic arms, and control the motion of CNC machines and lathes. They are also the primary movers for heavy-duty applications like elevators, lifts, and cranes, where their high starting torque is essential.³²
Medical and Renewable Energy

: The reliability of d.c. motors makes them vital in medical technology, where they are used in infusion pumps, ventilators, and electric wheelchairs. In the renewable energy sector, they are used to adjust the angle of solar panels, tracking the sun to maximize energy capture.³²

The design of these motors is tailored to their specific function. A heavy-duty motor for a crane or elevator will be designed with many turns, operate at high currents, and use powerful electromagnets to generate the necessary high torque.³³ In contrast, a small motor for a child's toy will use a much simpler design with fewer turns and weaker permanent magnets to provide motion at a lower cost and power consumption.³
Conclusion: A Synthesis of Principles

The journey to understand the d.c. motor begins with the fundamental physics of the motor effect—a linear force exerted on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field. The direction of this force is elegantly predicted by Fleming's Left-Hand Rule. Through clever engineering, this linear force is transformed into a rotational torque by shaping the wire into a coil. The challenge of continuous motion is solved by the ingenuity of the split-ring commutator, a self-timed mechanical switch that reverses the current every half-turn, ensuring the torque remains unidirectional. Finally, the power of this turning effect is not fixed; it can be precisely amplified by increasing the number of turns in the coil, increasing the current supplied to it, or increasing the strength of the magnetic field in which it operates. The d.c. motor is a powerful testament to human ingenuity, a device that seamlessly combines fundamental laws of physics into a machine that has become the invisible yet ever-present heart of motion in the modern world.
The Fundamental Interaction: Unveiling the Motor Effect
Defining the Phenomenon
At the heart of much of modern technology, from electric vehicles to household fans, lies a fundamental principle of electromagnetism known as the
motor effect

. This effect describes the observation that a conductor carrying an electric current will experience a mechanical force when it is placed within an external magnetic field.¹ This is not a passive interaction; the magnetic field actively pushes or pulls on the wire, causing it to move.⁴ The motor effect is the foundational principle that facilitates the conversion of electrical energy into mechanical energy in the form of motion or rotation.¹

The conditions for this phenomenon are precise. A conductor placed within a magnetic field will experience no force if there is no current flowing through it.¹ The force is a direct result of the moving charges that constitute the current. Therefore, the presence of both a magnetic field and an electric current within that field are necessary prerequisites for the motor effect to occur.
The Physics of Interaction: A Deeper Look
To understand why this force arises, one must consider that it is the result of an interaction between two distinct magnetic fields.¹
The External Magnetic Field

: This is a pre-existing, and often uniform, magnetic field. In a typical laboratory or motor setup, this field is provided by permanent magnets, such as a large horseshoe magnet or a pair of bar magnets. The magnetic field is represented by field lines that travel from the magnet's north pole to its south pole.²
The Conductor's Magnetic Field

: It is a fundamental principle of electromagnetism that any wire carrying an electric current generates its own magnetic field.¹ This field consists of a series of concentric circles centred on the wire. The direction of this circular field can be determined using the right-hand grip rule.

When the current-carrying wire is placed within the external magnetic field, these two fields superimpose and interact. On one side of the wire, the direction of the wire's circular field will be the same as the direction of the external field. Here, the fields reinforce each other, creating a region of a stronger, denser magnetic field. On the opposite side of the wire, the wire's field opposes the external field. Here, the fields partially cancel each other out, creating a region of a weaker magnetic field. This asymmetry in the combined magnetic field creates a net force. The wire is pushed from the area of high magnetic field strength (where the fields add up) towards the area of low magnetic field strength (where they cancel), much like an object is pushed from a region of high pressure to low pressure. This provides a clear physical explanation for the origin of the force.

This force is not exerted on the wire material itself, but rather on the moving electric charges—the electrons—that constitute the current. The magnetic field exerts a tiny force on each individual electron flowing through the wire.⁴ The macroscopic force observed on the wire is the vector sum of these billions of microscopic forces acting in unison.¹⁰ This understanding unifies the motor effect on a wire with the force experienced by a single charged particle, such as a proton or electron, moving through a magnetic field.⁵
Conditions for the Force: Orientation Matters
The magnitude of the force experienced by the conductor is critically dependent on its orientation relative to the magnetic field lines.
Maximum Force

: The force is at its maximum when the conductor is positioned so that the current flows at a right angle (90°) to the direction of the magnetic field lines.¹ This perpendicular arrangement ensures the most effective interaction between the external field and the field generated by the current, producing the greatest possible push.⁹
Reduced Force

: If the wire is placed at any other angle to the magnetic field, the force will be less than the maximum.² Only the component of the current that is perpendicular to the magnetic field contributes to the force.
Zero Force

: If the wire is aligned parallel to the magnetic field lines, it will experience no force at all.² In this orientation, the circular magnetic field around the wire does not create the necessary regions of reinforcement and cancellation with the external field to produce a net force.¹⁰
Mastering Direction: A Practical Guide to Fleming's Left-Hand Rule
Introduction to the Rule
While understanding the interaction of magnetic fields explains why a force exists, a practical tool is needed to predict its direction. This tool is
Fleming's Left-Hand Rule

, a mnemonic developed in the late 19th century by English electrical engineer John Ambrose Fleming.⁷ The rule provides a simple and reliable method for determining the direction of the force (often called thrust or motion) when the directions of the magnetic field and the conventional current are known.⁵ It is essential to recognise that the rule indicates only the direction of the force, not its magnitude.⁷

A defining characteristic of the relationship described by this rule is that the three quantities—Force, Magnetic Field, and Current—are always mutually perpendicular, meaning they are all at right angles (90°) to each other.⁴ This geometric arrangement is why exam questions on this topic often involve three-dimensional thinking, with forces described as acting "into the page" or "out of the page".⁸
A Practical, Step-by-Step Application Guide

To apply Fleming's Left-Hand Rule correctly, one must physically orient their left hand according to a precise procedure. Using the hand as a physical model removes ambiguity and greatly increases accuracy, especially under exam conditions.
Orient your Left Hand
: Begin by extending the thumb, first finger (index finger), and second finger (middle finger) of your left hand so that they form three right angles, similar to a 3D coordinate axis.²
Align the Field Finger
: The first and most crucial step is to point your
F
irst finger in the direction of the magnetic
F
ield. This is the anchor for the entire process. Remember, magnetic field lines are always directed from a North pole to a South pole.²
Align the Current Finger
: While keeping your first finger fixed in the direction of the magnetic field, rotate your hand and wrist until your se
C
ond finger points in the direction of the conventional
C
urrent. Conventional current is defined as flowing from the positive (+) terminal of a power source to the negative (−) terminal.¹
Read the Force Direction
: With the first and second fingers correctly aligned, your
Th
umb will now automatically point in the direction of the resulting
Th
rust or
F
orce.² This is the direction in which the wire will be pushed and begin to move.
To aid memory, the mnemonic "Father, Mother, Child" can be used, corresponding to Force (Thumb), Magnetic Field (First Finger), and Current (Second Finger).¹⁴

An Important Distinction: Conventional Current vs. Electron Flow
A common point of confusion for students arises from the two ways of describing electric current. Fleming's Left-Hand Rule is defined using
conventional current
, which is the historical convention describing current as the flow of positive charge from a positive terminal to a negative one.³
In reality, in a metallic conductor, the charge carriers are negatively charged electrons, which flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. Therefore, the direction of
electron flow
is always opposite to the direction of conventional current.⁴
When a problem involves a beam of electrons or other negative particles, a crucial adjustment must be made:
The second (Current) finger must be pointed in the direction

to the motion of the negative charges.⁴

This distinction highlights the duality in electromagnetism. The Left-Hand Rule is applied when an electric current (the cause) produces a force (the effect), as in an electric motor. Its counterpart, the Right-Hand Rule, is used in generators where motion (the cause) induces a current (the effect).⁷ Recognising this cause-and-effect relationship provides a robust conceptual framework for deciding which rule to apply.
Quantifying the Force: Factors and Calculation
Qualitative Analysis: How to Increase the Force
The magnitude of the force produced by the motor effect is not fixed; it can be altered by changing several key parameters of the system. A stronger force can be generated by:
Increasing the current (I)

: A larger current flowing through the conductor generates a stronger magnetic field around it. This leads to a more powerful interaction with the external field and, consequently, a larger resultant force.¹
Increasing the strength of the external magnetic field (B)
: Using more powerful permanent magnets or a stronger electromagnet creates a denser external magnetic field. This stronger field exerts a greater push on the current-carrying wire.¹
Increasing the length of the conductor in the field (L)

: The total force is the sum of the forces on all the moving charges within the field. Therefore, a longer section of wire placed within the magnetic field will experience a greater overall force.³ In practical applications like motors, this is often achieved by winding the wire into a coil with many turns; more turns mean a greater effective length of wire interacting with the field.⁶
The Force Equation (F=BIL)
The relationship between these factors is formalised by a simple and powerful equation, which applies when the current is perpendicular to the magnetic field ²:
F = B × I × L
Each term in this equation has a precise definition and standard unit:
F
is the
Force
experienced by the conductor, measured in

This equation is more than just a tool for calculation; it is a statement of direct proportionality. This means, for instance, that if the current is doubled while all other factors remain constant, the force will also double. If the magnetic field strength is tripled and the length of the wire in the field is halved, the new force will be 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 times the original force. This type of proportional reasoning is a higher-order skill essential for predicting how changes in a system will affect its behaviour, a common requirement in "describe and explain" exam questions.
Worked Calculation
Applying the formula requires careful attention to units, as values are often given in non-SI units like centimetres (cm) or milliamperes (mA).

F=BIL
